title: Token-level Tracing & Runtime Profiling — Equinox Dynamics Deep Dive
summary: SE-led deep dive on integrating token-level telemetry into Equinox's on-prem inference runtime. Covered KV cache visibility, batching effects on latency, quantized model profiling, and OpenTelemetry span design for token metrics. Agreed to run a pilot trace run in Equinox staging and share a lightweight dashboard template.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-02-11 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Noah (Redwood Infra), Priya (Equinox Head ML), Oliver (Platform), Samira (Security)

[00:00:00] Ethan: alright everyone thanks for taking the time, quick intro, i'll hand over to maya for the deep dive, we wanted to focus on trace/telemetry patterns that are useful when you run inference on-prem and at token granularity

[00:00:18] Maya: thanks ethan. so high level goal: get token-level observability without exploding cardinality or network overhead. we'll show a few patterns we've used at other customers, and then discuss how that maps to your VPC/on-prem constraints

[00:00:45] Priya: quick context — we run a mixture of 8x A100 pods in our colo for inference, most models are quantized to int8 but we also have a small fp16 fleet for accuracy-sensitive routes. latency SLO is 120ms p95 for chat flows. current issue is seeing jitter when we hit mid sized batches, and we have little visibility into the KV cache hit patterns

[00:01:10] Maya: okay good, that helps. first pattern: use OTEL spans at request and token layers. create a request span (rpc) that contains child spans for model_decode and kv_lookup. token spans are sampled: not every token, but strategy is head/tail sampling + deterministic sampling for tokens around completion boundaries

[00:01:42] Oliver: when you say token spans, are we talking one span per token? seems like that could be high cardinality and blow up our collector

[00:01:55] Maya: exactly the main tradeoff. we recommend emitting aggregated token metrics as metrics (counters/histograms) and only emit detailed traces for sampled requests. e.g. token_length histogram, token_index distribution, and a small number of token-span traces per minute. also prefix caching: instrument kv_lookup with attributes like kv_key_length, cache_hit=true/false, bucketed_latency_ms

[00:02:30] Samira: from security side we need to avoid logging PII or message content in spans. is it safe to put token text in attributes?

[00:02:40] Noah: short answer: no. we strip token text. we use token ids and hashed prefixes if needed for debug, and we rely on deterministic local sampling to replay if requested under a security process

[00:03:05] Maya: demo slide — here's an otel span model: trace -> request_span (attributes: route, model_name, model_version, batch_size, tenant) -> child spans model_decode (attrs: tokens_output, decode_time_ms), kv_lookup (attrs: cache_hit, key_bucket, kv_latency_ms), io (attrs: src, bytes). for token metrics we push counters to a Prometheus-compatible backend: tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hits_total, per-route_latency_ms buckets

[00:03:45] Priya: can you explain how batching changes these metrics? we see p99 spikes when we go from batch size 1 to 8

[00:03:57] Maya: yes batching affects tail latency. when you batch, queuing delay adds to token latency and kv cache warmup behaves differently. patterns: 1) record queue_time_ms as its own metric, 2) record model_compute_ms per-token and per-batch, 3) keep KV cache metrics with batch-awareness: kv_lookups_per_request, kv_hits_per_batch. that way you can see if spikes are due to queuing or model compute

[00:04:30] Oliver: do you have examples of dashboards that break down queue_time vs compute vs kv?

[00:04:38] Maya: yes, we'll share a dashboard template (link in notes). typical panels: time series for request rate, batch size distribution, queue_time_ms p95/p99, model_compute_ms heatmap, kv_cache_hit rate, token_output_per_second. also a flamegraph-like view derived from sampled traces to show where time is spent inside a request

[00:05:10] Priya: about quantization — our int8 models are faster but sometimes hallucinate more or differ in token timing. can we surface that in telemetry?

[00:05:22] Maya: absolutely — we attach model_profile tags: quant_level=int8|fp16, and emit quality metrics from eval prompts (tracked separately) and correlate with latency. for runtime, quantized kernels often reduce compute_ms but may increase memory bandwidth; so record model_kernel_ms and kernel_name attribute (e.g., matmul_opt_v2_q8). we also recommend periodic microbenchmarks under your exact sequence length distribution to generate kernel-level baselines

[00:05:55] Samira: for on-prem/VPC — our security team wants minimal egress. how does OTEL exporting work? do we need to run a local collector?

[00:06:05] Noah: yes we usually run an OTEL collector inside the VPC and forward only aggregated metrics and sampled traces to the RD hosted observability or your internal backend. Redwood supports local collector config and you can disable payload exports; we also support S3-style log upload behind your firewall for audit logs

[00:06:28] Maya: note on telemetry volume: token-level metrics naive approach = tokens_per_second * attributes -> huge. so we compress: histogram buckets for token latency, cardinality bounding on attributes (bucket key sizes), and use attribute set sampling. also prefix/KV cache metrics are aggregated at shard level rather than per-token where possible

[00:07:05] [demo noise — screen share mentioned: otel span examples and prometheus rules]

[00:07:20] Oliver: you mentioned deterministic sampling. can you explain how we can reproduce a trace given sampling? important for debugging production incidents

[00:07:30] Maya: deterministic sampling uses a stable hash of request ID + tenant ID modulo sample rate. if a sampled request is flagged for replay we can re-run it in staging with cache warmup. we keep a limited set of trace snapshots (stripped of user content) tied to the hashed ids for 7 days by default

[00:07:50] Priya: curious about KV cache visibility. right now we can't see which keys hit vs missed across pods; sometimes one pod's cold cache causes client-visible latency spikes

[00:08:05] Noah: we instrument the cache shard to emit per-shard metrics: cache_capacity, cache_evictions, cache_hit_ratio, average_lookup_ms. also emit a small sampled trace when we see cross-shard misses to identify hot keys. we bucket keys by prefix length to avoid cardinality explosion (e.g., prefix_8bucket 0-255)

[00:08:40] Maya: another practical tip: expose a 'kv_warmup' metric during rollout — when a new model version is deployed, run a synthetic warmup trace that primes the KV cache and emit warmup_completion_time. that helps explain early-traffic spikes after rollout

[00:09:05] Priya: about instrumentation code — what libraries do you recommend? we use python flask/gunicorn for the API and a separate C++ inference server for the runtime

[00:09:15] Maya: for python API use otel-python with Prometheus exporter. instrument the API handler and the client to the inference server. for C++ runtime, use OpenTelemetry C++ SDK and a lightweight export path to a local collector. Redwood's runtime has hooks that emit trace context and token/kv events via a small C API — we can share a sample wrapper for your runtime (we will send the repo link)

[00:09:50] Oliver: is there an example of the sampling config we can copy?

[00:09:56] Maya: yes we'll share a sampling.yaml with deterministic hash rules, head/tail token sampling, and rules for error-only high-fidelity traces. we'll also include retention guidelines so you don't store token-level traces forever

[00:10:15] Priya: can telemetry help root cause those p99 spikes? sometimes we just see 'model took long' which isn't actionable

[00:10:25] Maya: yes the combination of queue_time_ms, model_kernel_ms, kv_lookup_ms in the same trace lets you pivot: if queue_time dominates then scaling/autoscaling policy needs tuning; if kv_lookup dominates then maybe cache sharding or TTL adjustments; if model_kernel dominates then quant/kernel choice or sequence length optimizations

[00:11:00] [15 minute marker omitted to keep note concise — conversation continues with concrete examples and small code snippets read aloud]

[00:26:30] Maya: here's a concrete example of a sampled trace: request_span (route: chat_v2, batch_size:4) -> model_decode (decode_time_ms:42) -> token_span #1 (token_index:0, token_latency_ms:3) -> kv_lookup (cache_hit:false, kv_latency_ms:12) -> token_span #5 (token_index:5, token_latency_ms:7, sampled=true). note: we don't include token text

[00:30:10] Priya: what about dashboards — do you provide templated Grafana panels for this?

[00:30:20] Maya: yes, repo link will include Grafana json for: p95/p99 latency panels, batch size heatmap, kv hit-rate by shard, kernel-level latency treemap, tokens/sec vs compute utilization. we'll also include an alert rule template for sustained queue_time p95 > 50ms

[00:31:00] Priya: quick question on compliance — Samira: how long are traces kept and do you support encryption-at-rest and KMS?

[00:31:10] Samira: we need SOC2-type controls and the ability to purge traces for a tenant on request

[00:31:22] Noah: Redwood supports encrypted storage, KMS integration for hosted telemetry, and for private we recommend keeping collectors and trace storage behind your KMS. trace retention is configurable per-tenant; we can implement purge APIs or legal hold flags. we'll share the security doc and SOC2 whitepaper

[00:31:50] Maya: small gotcha: if you want to tie token-level regressions to model changes, put model_git_sha or model_build_id on the request span. then you can correlate regressions with rollouts

[00:32:20] Oliver: can we run these traces in staging without affecting prod latency?

[00:32:28] Maya: yes run them against a mirrored traffic lane or replay traffic at reduced rate. for the KV warmup we run synthetic batches that mimic your sequence length distribution to avoid skew

[00:33:00] Priya: what about cost — does this telemetry massively increase costs? we are sensitive to storage and egress

[00:33:10] Maya: it's a cost tradeoff. default approach: aggregated metrics + sampled traces keeps costs low. token-level histograms are cheap; full token traces are expensive. optimizing retention and sampling rate will be the biggest lever; also local ingestion and downsampling in the collector reduces egress costs

[00:34:00] [Maya shares a link: https://redwood.example.com/telemetry-templates/token-trace-dashboard ]

[00:34:20] Priya: can you show an example alert rule for cache evictions?

[00:34:30] Maya: example: alert if cache_eviction_rate per-shard > 0.01 for 5m AND cache_hit_ratio < 0.85. cause: hot keys or undersized shard. mitigation: increase shard size or pre-warm top keys

[00:35:05] Oliver: one more thing — we use multi-tenant shards. how do you avoid tenant bleed in metrics?

[00:35:15] Maya: add tenant_id attr at the request span but avoid making it high-cardinality in metrics. instead use tenant buckets for top-N tenants and aggregate the rest into 'other'. for traces, keep tenant id only in secure storage with access controls

[00:35:40] Priya: ok this is helpful. what's the recommended pilot?

[00:35:48] Ethan: recommended pilot: 2-week run in staging with otel-collector deployed, shallow token sampling enabled, run synthetic warmup for model rollout, export metrics to your Grafana. scope: validate queue_time, kv-miss correlation, and one quantized model profile

[00:36:10] Priya: timeline — target pilot next week, we'd need Redwood's sampling config and dashboard template

[00:36:20] Maya: will share sampling.yaml, Grafana json, and a C++ wrapper for the runtime's trace hooks. we'll also send a short security FAQ

[00:36:35] Samira: one final question — do you have any examples of root-cause where telemetry revealed a surprising cause?

[00:36:45] Maya: yes one customer saw p99 spikes caused by cache evictions from a background job that compressed caches during night window; telemetry showed kv_eviction spikes exactly aligned with p99 windows. fixing the job schedule solved it. another case: quantized kernel had a pathological slow path for sequence length 1024 causing token latency to double; kernel-level metrics found it

[00:37:15] [wrap-up — recap and next steps]

[00:37:25] Ethan: recap: we will send sampling config, dashboard, C++ wrapper, security docs; Equinox to stand up collector in staging and run pilot. agreed target to start pilot 2026-02-18.

[00:37:40] Priya: sounds good — i'll coordinate internal infra and send calendar invite to confirm the 18th

[00:37:48] Oliver: thanks all, appreciate the concrete examples

[00:37:52] Maya: thanks everyone.

[00:58:00] [call ends — final minutes include light chat about upcoming conferences and follow-ups]
